title: Grammar & Verbal Ability
weightage: 5-8 questions (the grammar-in-context cluster of Language I, both Paper I and II)
intro: Language I English on the CTET is not a grammar exam in the school sense — it is a grammar-in-context exam. You will not be asked to define a gerund. Instead a short passage, a poem or a single sentence is put in front of you and a word is blanked out, an error is buried in one of four underlined parts, or a sentence has to be turned from active to passive. The skill the paper rewards is recognising the correct form fast, in running text, the way a literate teacher would when marking a child's notebook. That is why the same six areas come back paper after paper: tenses, parts of speech, articles and prepositions, voice and narration, subject-verb agreement, and word knowledge (synonyms, antonyms, word formation). This chapter drills each one the CTET way — the rule in one tight paragraph, then the exact question shapes (fill-in-the-blank, spot-the-error, transformation, closest-in-meaning) you will actually face. Master these and you also lift your comprehension-passage score, because the questions there test the very same forms.

items.name: Simple Present
items.formula: V1 / V1+s · habit, fact -> She writes daily.

items.name: Present Continuous
items.formula: is/am/are + V-ing · now -> She is writing.

items.name: Present Perfect
items.formula: has/have + V3 · past with present link -> She has written.

items.name: Past Continuous
items.formula: was/were + V-ing · ongoing past -> She was writing.

items.name: Past Perfect
items.formula: had + V3 · earlier of two past actions -> She had written before he came.

items.name: Simple Future
items.formula: will + V1 · later -> She will write.

items.name: Articles a / an
items.formula: By SOUND not letter -> a university, an hour, an MP, a one-rupee coin.

items.name: Article the
items.formula: Specific / unique / superlative -> the sun, the best, the book you read.

items.name: Subject-verb agreement
items.formula: Verb agrees with the SUBJECT, not the nearest noun -> The box of pens is here.

items.name: Active -> Passive
items.formula: Object becomes subject + be + V3 -> Ram ate it / It was eaten by Ram.

items.name: Direct -> Indirect
items.formula: Backshift tense, shift pronouns & time words -> said, "I am here" / said that he was there.

items.name: Each / every / either / neither
items.formula: Always SINGULAR verb -> Each boy was present.

topics.name: Tenses
topics.details: Tense is the single most frequent grammar point in Language I, and the CTET almost never asks it in isolation. It hides a tense inside a sentence and asks you to fill the blank with the form that fits the time signal and the rest of the sentence. The clues are time-words and structure: a habit or general truth takes simple present (Water boils at 100 degrees), an action happening now takes present continuous, and an action started in the past with a result that still matters takes present perfect (often signalled by since, for, already, just, yet). Two traps recur. First, sequence of past actions: when one past action happened before another, the earlier one takes past perfect (had + V3) and the later one simple past -- The train had left before we reached. Second, the conditional and reported-speech contexts where a present tense must be back-shifted. In the comprehension section the same skill appears as identifying why a writer used a particular tense, so reading the time-frame of the whole sentence, not just the blank, is the habit to build.

solved.problem: Fill in the blank: 'By the time the bell rang, the children ____ their lunch.' (finish)
solved.solution: had finished. Two past actions; the eating finished BEFORE the bell rang, so the earlier action takes the past perfect (had + V3).

solved.problem: Fill in the blank: 'She ____ in this school since 2015.' (teach)
solved.solution: has taught (or has been teaching). 'Since 2015' signals an action that began in the past and continues to the present -- the present perfect.

solved.problem: Choose the correct form: 'Look! The baby ____ (cry).'
solved.solution: is crying. 'Look!' signals an action happening at this very moment, which takes the present continuous (is + V-ing).

solved.problem: Identify the error: 'Water boiled at 100 degrees Celsius.'
solved.solution: 'boiled' is wrong; a universal/scientific fact takes the simple present -- 'Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.'

unsolved.problem: Fill in the blank: 'They ____ (watch) television when the power went off.'
hints: One action was in progress when another interrupted it.

unsolved.problem: Fill in the blank: 'I ____ (already / eat) when you called.'
hints: One past action happened before another.

unsolved.problem: Choose the correct form: 'The earth ____ (revolve) around the sun.'
hints: It is a permanent, universal truth.
Universal truths take the simple present.

unsolved.problem: Fill in the blank: 'He ____ (live) in Delhi for ten years now.'
hints: "for ten years now" links past to present.

topics.name: Parts of Speech
topics.details: The CTET tests parts of speech functionally -- it underlines a word in a sentence and asks what part of speech it is THERE, because the same word changes category by use. 'Light' is a noun in 'turn off the light', a verb in 'light the lamp', and an adjective in 'a light bag'. So the rule to drill is: decide by the work the word does in this sentence, not by a fixed label. Quick functional tests help. A noun names (and can take a/an/the before it); a pronoun replaces a noun (he, it, themselves); a verb shows action or state and can be marked for tense; an adjective describes a noun (which one? what kind? how many?); an adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb and often answers how/when/where (many, not all, end in -ly); a preposition shows relation (in, on, between); a conjunction joins (and, but, because); an interjection exclaims (Oh! Alas!). The frequent trap is the adjective-versus-adverb pair (She sings beautiful vs beautifully) and treating every -ly word as an adverb -- friendly, lovely and lonely are adjectives.

solved.problem: What part of speech is the underlined word: 'She gave a *fast* reply.'
solved.solution: Adjective. 'fast' describes the noun 'reply' (what kind of reply), so it is functioning as an adjective here, not an adverb.

solved.problem: Identify the part of speech of 'but' in: 'He is poor but honest.'
solved.solution: Conjunction. 'but' joins two adjectives/ideas, so it is a (coordinating) conjunction.

solved.problem: Correct the error: 'She speaks English very fluent.'
solved.solution: 'fluent' should be 'fluently'. It modifies the verb 'speaks' (how she speaks), so it must be an adverb: 'She speaks English very fluently.'

solved.problem: What part of speech is the underlined word: 'The *poor* need our help.'
solved.solution: Noun. Preceded by 'the' and acting as the subject, 'poor' here names a group of people, so it functions as a noun.

unsolved.problem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word: 'He ran *quickly* to the gate.'
What part of speech is 'under' in: 'The cat is under the table.'?
hints: It shows the relation between cat and table.
in / on / under / between belong to one class.

unsolved.problem: Spot the error: 'She is a very friendly and lovely child.' -- which class are friendly and lovely?
hints: Do not be fooled by the -ly ending.

unsolved.problem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word in 'Wow! That was a brilliant catch.' (the word Wow)
hints: It stands apart with an exclamation mark.

topics.name: Articles & Prepositions
topics.details: Articles and prepositions are the small words the CTET loves to blank out, because they catch even confident readers. The article rule that the paper tests is sound, not spelling: use 'a' before a consonant SOUND and 'an' before a vowel SOUND -- so it is 'a university' and 'a one-rupee note' (they begin with a 'yoo' and 'wun' sound) but 'an hour', 'an honest man' and 'an MP' (silent h, and 'em' begins with a vowel sound). 'The' marks something specific, already mentioned, unique (the sun, the Ganga), or a superlative (the tallest). Prepositions are tested mainly as fixed usage and collocation -- the choice that sounds right to a fluent ear: good AT maths, afraid OF dogs, married TO, depend ON, different FROM, congratulate someone ON. Time and place prepositions follow a size ladder: 'at' for points (at 5 o'clock, at the door), 'on' for days and surfaces (on Monday, on the wall), 'in' for longer periods and enclosed spaces (in June, in Delhi, in the box). The CTET blank usually has exactly one collocation that a literate speaker would accept, so trust the standard partnership.

solved.problem: Fill in the blank: 'He is ____ honest officer and ____ university topper.'
solved.solution: an honest, a university. 'honest' begins with a silent h (vowel sound) so it takes 'an'; 'university' begins with a 'yoo' (consonant) sound so it takes 'a'.

solved.problem: Fill in the blank: 'She is very good ____ mathematics.'
solved.solution: at. The fixed collocation is 'good at' (a subject/skill). 'good in' is non-standard here.

solved.problem: Fill in the blank: 'The meeting is ____ Monday ____ 10 o'clock.'
solved.solution: on Monday, at 10 o'clock. Days take 'on'; clock-time points take 'at'.

solved.problem: Identify the error: 'I have been waiting since two hours.'
solved.solution: 'since' should be 'for'. 'since' is used with a point in time (since 2 p.m.); 'for' is used with a duration (for two hours).

unsolved.problem: Fill in the blank: 'It took us ____ hour to reach ____ railway station.'
hints: "hour" begins with a silent h -> vowel sound.
"railway station" is a specific, known place.

unsolved.problem: Fill in the blank: 'My answer is quite different ____ yours.'
Fill in the blank: 'The book is ____ the table and the keys are ____ the drawer.'
unsolved.answer: on the table, in the drawer

unsolved.problem: Spot the error: 'She is married with a doctor.'
hints: You are married TO a person.
unsolved.answer: with should be to (married to a doctor)

topics.name: Active/Passive Voice & Narration
topics.details: Transformation questions -- change this sentence from active to passive, or from direct to indirect speech -- are a CTET staple because they test whether a teacher truly controls sentence structure. For VOICE, the move is mechanical once learned: the object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive, the verb becomes the matching form of 'be' + the past participle (V3), and the old subject moves to a 'by' phrase (often dropped if unimportant). 'The teacher praised the boy' becomes 'The boy was praised (by the teacher)'. Keep the tense the same -- present perfect active maps to present perfect passive (has eaten -> has been eaten). For NARRATION, reporting another's exact words as indirect speech needs three shifts: back-shift the tense one step into the past when the reporting verb is past (am -> was, will -> would, can -> could), change pronouns to match the new speaker's point of view, and shift time/place words (now -> then, today -> that day, here -> there, this -> that). Questions become statements introduced by asked/enquired (Wh- keep the question word; yes/no use if/whether), and commands use a 'to'-infinitive after told/ordered/requested.

solved.problem: Change to passive voice: 'The mason is building a wall.'
solved.solution: 'A wall is being built (by the mason).' Present continuous active -> 'is/are being + V3' in the passive; object 'a wall' becomes the subject.

solved.problem: Change to passive voice: 'Somebody has stolen my bicycle.'
solved.solution: 'My bicycle has been stolen.' Present perfect maps to 'has/have been + V3'; the vague agent 'somebody' is dropped.

solved.problem: Change to indirect speech: She said, 'I am writing a letter now.'
solved.solution: She said that she was writing a letter then. Back-shift 'am' -> 'was', change 'I' -> 'she', and 'now' -> 'then'.

solved.problem: Change to indirect speech: He said to me, 'Please help me.'
solved.solution: He requested me to help him. A polite command/request uses 'requested + object + to-infinitive'; 'me' (his) -> 'him'.

unsolved.problem: Change to passive voice: 'The children are flying kites.'
hints: Present continuous passive = is/are being + V3.
unsolved.answer: Kites are being flown (by the children).

unsolved.problem: Change to passive voice: 'Who wrote this letter?'
unsolved.answer: By whom was this letter written?

unsolved.problem: Change to indirect speech: The teacher said to the students, 'Do not make noise.'
unsolved.answer: The teacher ordered/told the students not to make noise.

unsolved.problem: Change to indirect speech: He said, 'I will come tomorrow.'
unsolved.answer: He said that he would come the next day.

topics.name: Subject-Verb Agreement
topics.details: Subject-verb agreement is the classic spot-the-error topic: a singular subject needs a singular verb and a plural subject a plural verb, but the CTET buries the real subject so the wrong verb looks right. The number-one trap is the phrase between subject and verb -- 'The box of chocolates IS on the table' (the subject is 'box', singular, not 'chocolates'). Learn the fixed cases. Words like each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody, nobody and 'one of' are always singular: 'Each of the boys WAS present.' Two subjects joined by 'and' are plural, but 'either...or' / 'neither...nor' / 'or' make the verb agree with the NEARER subject -- 'Neither the teacher nor the students WERE informed.' A collective noun (team, family, government, jury) usually takes a singular verb when acting as one unit. Uncountable nouns (news, information, furniture, advice) and certain nouns ending in -s but singular in meaning (mathematics, physics, news) take a singular verb -- 'The news IS good.' Some words look singular but are plural -- 'scissors', 'trousers' and 'a pair of...' take a plural verb. Reading to the true headword before choosing the verb is the whole game.

solved.problem: Correct the sentence: 'The list of items are on the desk.'
solved.solution: 'The list of items IS on the desk.' The subject is 'list' (singular); 'of items' is a modifier and does not change the verb.

solved.problem: Choose the correct verb: 'Neither the principal nor the teachers ____ (was/were) available.'
solved.solution: were. With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the NEARER subject, which is 'teachers' (plural).

solved.problem: Correct the sentence: 'Each of the students have a book.'
solved.solution: 'Each of the students HAS a book.' 'Each' is always singular, so the verb is 'has', not 'have'.

solved.problem: Choose the correct verb: 'Mathematics ____ (is/are) my favourite subject.'
solved.solution: is. Though it ends in -s, 'mathematics' is a singular subject (a field of study), so it takes a singular verb.

unsolved.problem: Spot and correct the error: 'One of my friends are a doctor.'
unsolved.answer: One of my friends IS a doctor.

unsolved.problem: Choose the correct verb: 'The news ____ (was/were) shocking.'
hints: Uncountable nouns take a singular verb.

unsolved.problem: Choose the correct verb: 'Either Ram or his brothers ____ (has/have) the keys.'
Spot and correct the error: 'My new trousers is too tight.'
unsolved.answer: My new trousers ARE too tight.

topics.name: Synonyms, Antonyms & Word Formation
topics.details: The vocabulary cluster asks for the word closest in meaning (synonym), the word opposite in meaning (antonym), or the right derived form (word formation), and on the CTET it is almost always set in a sentence so context decides the shade of meaning. For synonyms and antonyms the safe method is to read the word in its sentence, predict the meaning yourself, then match -- because many options are 'close but wrong'. For instance 'abundant' means plentiful (synonym) and its antonym is scarce; 'reluctant' means unwilling, opposite eager. Word formation tests how prefixes and suffixes build new parts of speech and meanings. Negative prefixes flip meaning: un- (happy/unhappy), in-/im-/il-/ir- (correct/incorrect, possible/impossible, legal/illegal, regular/irregular), dis- (agree/disagree), mis- (lead/mislead). Suffixes change the part of speech: -ness and -ity make nouns (kind/kindness, able/ability), -ful and -less make adjectives (care/careful/careless), -ly makes adverbs (quick/quickly), -ise/-ify make verbs (modern/modernise). The CTET reward here is precision: choose the prefix that actually pairs with the root (it is 'irregular', never 'unregular') and the synonym whose connotation fits the sentence.

solved.problem: Choose the word closest in meaning to 'abundant' in: 'The region has abundant rainfall.'
solved.solution: Plentiful. 'abundant' means present in large quantity; 'plentiful' is its synonym (its antonym would be 'scarce').

solved.problem: Choose the correct negative form: The opposite of 'legal' is ____.
solved.solution: illegal. Roots beginning with 'l' take the prefix 'il-' (il + legal), not 'un-' or 'in-'.

solved.problem: Give the antonym of 'reluctant' in: 'She was reluctant to leave.'
solved.solution: Eager (or willing). 'reluctant' means unwilling/hesitant, so its opposite is eager/willing.

solved.problem: Form a noun from the adjective 'happy'.
solved.solution: Happiness. The suffix '-ness' turns the adjective 'happy' into a noun (note the y -> i spelling change).

unsolved.problem: Choose the synonym of 'brave' in: 'The brave soldier saved them.'
hints: Think of a word for fearless.

unsolved.problem: Choose the antonym of 'ancient' in: 'They studied ancient ruins.'
Choose the correct negative form: The opposite of 'regular' is ____.
Form an adverb from the adjective 'careful'.

shortcuts: Tense by time-signal: since/for/already/just/yet -> present perfect; while/when (background) -> past continuous; one past action before another -> past perfect (had + V3).
a vs an goes by SOUND, not letter: a university, a one-rupee coin (consonant sounds) vs an hour, an honest man, an MP (vowel sounds).
In spot-the-error SVA questions, cross out everything between the subject and the verb, then check agreement -- the noun nearest the verb is usually a decoy.
Active -> Passive recipe: Object first, then the right form of BE + V3, then "by + old subject". Tense never changes.
Direct -> Indirect (past reporting verb): back-shift the tense one step, change pronouns to the reporter, and shift time/place words (now->then, today->that day, here->there).
each / every / either / neither / one of / a pair of subject -> SINGULAR verb; either-or / neither-nor -> verb agrees with the NEARER subject.
mistakes: Using "since" for a duration -- it is "for two hours" (duration) but "since 2 o-clock" (point in time).
Treating every -ly word as an adverb -- friendly, lovely, lonely, silly are adjectives.
Choosing the article by the first LETTER instead of the first SOUND (writing "an university" or "a hour").
Making the verb agree with the noun nearest it instead of the true subject ("The box of pens are" -- should be "is").
Forgetting to back-shift the tense or to change "this/now/here" when converting direct speech to indirect.
Picking the wrong negative prefix -- it is "irregular", "illegal", "impossible", not "unregular/unlegal/unpossible".
pyq: In Language I English, this grammar-in-context cluster typically supplies five to eight marks across both papers, and it overlaps heavily with the comprehension passages. The most frequent question shapes are: fill-in-the-blank with the correct tense or preposition; spot-the-error in one of four underlined parts (subject-verb agreement and article/preposition errors dominate); transformation (active <-> passive, direct <-> indirect speech); and the closest-in-meaning / opposite-in-meaning pair tested inside a sentence. High-yield recurring items: present-perfect with since/for, past perfect for the earlier of two past actions, a/an by sound, married to / good at / different from collocations, neither-nor agreement with the nearer subject, passive of perfect tenses, and negative-prefix word formation (il-/im-/ir-/in-). Because the same forms are tested again in the reading passage, mastering this chapter raises the whole Language I score, not just the standalone grammar items.

flashcards.q: When do we use the present perfect tense?
flashcards.a: A past action linked to the present; signals since, for, already, just, yet -> has/have + V3.

flashcards.q: For two past actions, which takes the past perfect?
flashcards.a: The EARLIER action (had + V3); the later one takes simple past.
a university (consonant "yoo" sound); an hour (silent h -> vowel sound). Go by SOUND.

flashcards.q: Which preposition: good ___ maths, afraid ___ dogs, different ___ this?
flashcards.a: good AT, afraid OF, different FROM.

flashcards.q: How do you turn an active sentence into passive?
flashcards.a: Object becomes subject + correct form of BE + V3 + (by + old subject); tense unchanged.

flashcards.q: Three changes when making direct speech indirect (past reporting verb)?
flashcards.a: Back-shift the tense, change the pronouns, shift time/place words (now->then, here->there).

flashcards.q: What verb does "each of the boys" take?
flashcards.a: Singular -- "Each of the boys IS/WAS...". each/every/either/neither are singular.

flashcards.q: With "neither...nor", the verb agrees with which subject?
flashcards.a: The NEARER subject (the one closest to the verb).
Singular verb -- "The news IS good", "Mathematics IS easy".

flashcards.q: Is every word ending in -ly an adverb?
flashcards.a: No -- friendly, lovely, lonely, silly are ADJECTIVES.

flashcards.q: Negative prefix for legal, regular, possible, mature?
flashcards.a: illegal, irregular, impossible, immature (il-/ir-/im-, not un-).

summary: CTET Language I English tests grammar in context across six areas. Tenses: read the time-signal (since/for/already -> present perfect; the earlier of two past actions -> past perfect; universal truths -> simple present). Parts of speech: decide by the word's FUNCTION in the sentence, and do not assume every -ly word is an adverb. Articles and prepositions: a/an by SOUND, the for specific things, and trust fixed collocations (good at, married to, different from, on Monday, at 5 o'clock). Voice and narration: passive = object + BE + V3 + by-agent with the tense kept; indirect speech = back-shift tense, change pronouns, shift time/place words. Subject-verb agreement: match the verb to the true subject, remember each/every/either/neither are singular, and neither-nor agrees with the nearer subject. Vocabulary and word formation: pick synonyms/antonyms by sentence context and use the correct negative prefix (il-/im-/ir-/in-/dis-/mis-). Mastering these lifts the comprehension score too, since the same forms recur there.
